name: Domaine la Barroche Châteauneuf-du-Pape Pure Rouge 2016
text:
## Domaine la Barroche Châteauneuf-du-Pape Pure Rouge 2016

**The story.** Domaine la Barroche is both one of the oldest family estates in [Châteauneuf-du-Pape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC) and one of its newest stars. Its roots go back to the 17th century, when Alexandre Barrot began acquiring land in the village; the same family has owned it ever since. For a long time it was small: in 1972, when Christian Barrot began expanding, it had just over 2 hectares, and the grapes were sold to merchants. Everything changed when his son Julien joined in 2002. From the 2003 vintage people began to notice, and from 2006, when Julien took on much more responsibility, the estate rose fast. His sister Laetitia Barrot Latour now helps him run it. In 2015 the family completely renovated the cellars, adding conical concrete vats ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/barroche-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**The vineyards.** Barroche owns about 15.5 hectares in Châteauneuf, mostly in the north of the appellation, on stony and sandy soils, with some [limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone), red clay and iron-rich [sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone). Its finest parcels are on sand right next to the legendary [Château Rayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Rayas) ([see the area from above](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+Rayas,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k)). The vines average more than 70 years old, some over 100. [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache) dominates, with smaller plantings of [Mourvèdre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourv%C3%A8dre), [Syrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrah), [Cinsault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinsaut), [Clairette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clairette_blanche), [Vaccarèse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brun_Argent%C3%A9), [Terret Noir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terret_noir) and [Clairette Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clairette_rose). The grapes are sorted twice, partly destemmed, and some Grenache is fermented as whole bunches; each variety then ages in the vessel that suits it best: concrete, small barrels or large foudres ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/barroche-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**The wine: Pure.** As the name says, Pure is 97 to 100% old-vine [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache), depending on the year, and even the label is stark white. It comes from pure sandy soils in the Grand Pierre, Rayas and Pointu lieux-dits, close to Château Rayas, from vines planted back in 1901. The grapes are partly destemmed and fermented in concrete, then the wine ages for about 18 months in one large, old oak foudre. Fewer than 300 cases are made a year, so it is hard to find ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/barroche-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**The vintage.** 2016 is one of the great modern years in the southern Rhône. [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/southern-rhone) quotes [Michel Chapoutier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapoutier) saying it could be better than the legendary 1990. Warm conditions all year and reduced yields gave wines of great concentration in colour, tannin and flavour, "certainly one of the great vintages" for reds, and safe for cellaring into the 2030s.

**What the critics say for 2016.**
- **Jeff Leve, [The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/barroche-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/): 100** (from the vintage list on his producer page, checked). A perfect score; Leve calls Barroche "one of the new super stars" of Châteauneuf.
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 95.2** (from your CellarTracker list). That is an exceptionally high community average, among the highest in your whole cellar.
- **Other critics.** Pure is made in such small amounts that few merchants list it. The importers' pages that quote other critics' notes for this vintage were blocked to me, so I can't confirm their scores; I'd rather leave them out than guess.

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is ten years old. Your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2024 to 2035, and The Wine Cellar Insider says the best Barroche vintages drink well from 8 to 20 years after the harvest. So this is in its prime now, with years to go. An old-vine Grenache from sand should be perfumed and silky at this age: red fruit, flowers, spice and [garrigue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrigue). Decant about an hour ahead, gently, and serve slightly cool.

**Serving.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests about 15.5°C, almost cellar temperature, and 1 to 2 hours in a [decanter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decantation) for younger bottles; older ones need only enough to leave the sediment behind. It says Barroche is usually best with 3 to 6 years in bottle, and the best vintages drink well from 8 to 20 years after the harvest ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/barroche-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**Food.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests classic meat dishes (veal, pork, beef, lamb, duck, game, roast chicken, braises, sausages, eggplant, tomatoes and [cassoulet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassoulet)), plus tuna, mushrooms and pasta. For a Grenache-led wine like this, my picks are a roast leg of lamb with [herbes de Provence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbes_de_Provence), duck breast with cherries, a [ratatouille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratatouille), or a [porcini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boletus_edulis) risotto. I'd avoid very spicy food.

**Value and where to buy.** None of the three stores on this site lists Barroche at the moment. Its top wines are made in tiny quantities and turn up mainly with fine-wine merchants and at auction.

**From the history books**
- **The popes and their castle.** In 1309 [Pope Clement V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_V), a former Archbishop of Bordeaux, moved the papacy to [Avignon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Palais+des+Papes,+Avignon,+France&t=k), beginning the [Avignon Papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_Papacy). His successor [John XXII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXII) improved the vineyards to the north and built the summer [castle](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+des+Papes,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) that gave the village its name, "the Pope's new castle". The wine became known as "Vin du Pape" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **Phylloxera.** The [phylloxera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_French_Wine_Blight) louse reached Châteauneuf in the early 1870s, earlier than most French regions, and wiped out the vineyards. Before the First World War, much of the replanted wine was sold to [Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundy_wine) as "vin de médecine" to strengthen thinner wines ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **France's first appellation.** Fraud was so common in the early 20th century that local growers, led by Baron [Pierre Le Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Le_Roy_de_Boiseaumari%C3%A9) of [Château Fortia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Fortia), drew up France's first [appellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appellation_d'origine_contr%C3%B4l%C3%A9e) rules in 1923, made law on 15 May 1936. One of the baron's rules: vines could only be planted on land dry enough to grow both [lavender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavandula) and [thyme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thyme) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **Three centuries of Barrots.** Barroche goes back to Alexandre Barrot's land purchases in the 17th century. Until 1972 the family's grapes were sold to merchants, under the name "Lou Destre d'Antan", a tribute to Christian Barrot's grandfather ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/barroche-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**Curious details**
- **Neighbours of a legend.** Barroche's best sandy parcels sit next to [Château Rayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Rayas). Wikipedia notes that some of the most prestigious vineyards in the appellation, like Rayas, look quite unlike the stony Châteauneuf of the postcards, with no big galets ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **Two versions of one wine.** For the 2007 vintage, Barroche bottled Pure twice, once filtered and once unfiltered, and there is no way to tell which one you're buying ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/barroche-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).
- **Liberty.** In 2015 Barroche added a wine called Liberty, blended from Châteauneuf and Côtes du Rhône vines. Because it mixes two appellations, the law says it can only be sold as plain [Vin de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Vin+de+France+wine&go=Go).
- **The famous stones.** Much of Châteauneuf is covered in [galets roulés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galets_roul%C3%A9s), smooth [quartzite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartz) stones left by Alpine glaciers and rounded over millennia by the [Rhône](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rh%C3%B4ne). They soak up the sun by day and give the heat back to the vines at night, and in dry summers they help keep moisture in the soil ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **The flying-cigar law.** In 1954, after local reports of [UFOs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_saucer), the Châteauneuf council banned "flying cigars" from flying over or landing in the commune. The decree is still in force, and a Californian Rhône-style wine from [Bonny Doon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonny_Doon_Vineyard), Le Cigare Volant, is named after the tale ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **Strong by law.** Châteauneuf must reach at least 12.5% alcohol with no added sugar, and most wines come in at 14 to 15.5%. Yields are limited to 35 hectolitres per hectare, nearly half what [Bordeaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bordeaux_wine) allows ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
